questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & -6 \\ 14 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Determine whether $A=PD{P}^{-1}$ for some invertible matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D,$ where $P$ and $D$ are both real. In the affirmative case, find a possible diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to determine whether $D$ is diagonalizable over $R.$

We start by computing the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 0 & -6 \\ 14 & 3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 3 & 0 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -6 \\ 3 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )+18) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +8) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For the quadratic polynomial  $\,{\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda +8\,$ we have that the discriminant $D<0.$ So, it doesn't have real roots. 

Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable over $R.$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & a & -2 \\ -1 & b & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the value of $(a+b)^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{2}I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 5 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -6\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 \\ 12 & -10 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 12 & -10 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st  and the $2$nd ones). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get  ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $(a+b)^{2}=(0+1)^{2}=1.$

questions.problem:
$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix $B$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}BP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}B-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-2I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-2)I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}B-4I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-4I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & ∗ \\ 0 & 1 & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the third column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ 

So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Computing $A-(4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{3}I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-(4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -6 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations whose augmented matrix $M$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix is already  in row echelon form.  It has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.  From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{2}(-4({x}_{3})-6{x}_{3}) \\  & =5{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}5{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 9 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

 
The matrix $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$
Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we are already given the eigenvalues of the matrix: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=6,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=7,\,$ ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ Applying our usual method, we get the following.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=6,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-7I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 & -4 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-9I)x=0$ gives us the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
